sessions.title: Welcome: the road to Emmaus
sessions.summary: Every journey of faith starts with Jesus walking beside us, often before we recognize him.
lesson: On the first Easter Sunday, two disciples walked home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, about seven miles (11 km) away. They were sad and confused: Jesus had died, and they did not understand the news that he was alive.

A stranger joined them on the road. He listened to them, then explained the Scriptures, showing how everything pointed to Jesus. When they reached the village they begged him, "Stay with us." At supper he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them. Their eyes were opened: it was Jesus.

Later they said to each other, "Were not our hearts burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?" That is the heart of this journey. You will hear the Scriptures, ask questions, walk with others, and come to the table of the Eucharist. Jesus is already walking with you, even on the days you do not see him.
You do not need to have everything figured out. The disciples on the road were full of doubts. Bring your questions; that is what this time is for.
sessions.reflection: What brought you to begin this journey? What are you hoping to find?

sessions.title: Prayer: talking with God
sessions.summary: Prayer is simply a conversation with God who loves you. Anyone can start today.
lesson: Prayer is lifting your heart and mind to God. It does not need special words; you can talk to God as you would to someone who loves you. Saint Thérèse of Lisieux called prayer "a surge of the heart, a simple look turned toward heaven."

Catholics pray in many ways: in our own words, with traditional prayers like the Our Father, with the Bible, in silence, and together at Mass. Traditional prayers are helpful when we do not know what to say; they have been prayed by millions of people before us.
When the disciples asked Jesus, "Lord, teach us to pray," he gave them the Our Father. It is the perfect place to start. Try praying it slowly once a day this week, thinking about each line.

A simple daily habit: when you wake up, make the Sign of the Cross and offer your day to God. Before sleep, think back over the day, thank God for one good thing, and say sorry for anything you regret.
sessions.reflection: What would help you make a few minutes of prayer part of your day?

sessions.title: The journey of faith: the Trinity, faith, and the God who is love
sessions.summary: God made us out of love, to share his life. He has shown us who he is: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

sources.title: Psalm 23, The Lord is my shepherd

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 1
lesson: This session opens with Psalm 23, "The Lord is my shepherd," alongside a picture of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus. Both say the same thing: we are not walking alone. God goes ahead of us, walks beside us, and leads us home.
## Psalm 23: the Lord is my shepherd
Your class handout prints the whole psalm. Here it is in the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible, where it is numbered Psalm 22. Your parish Bible will word it a little differently.

> The Lord ruleth me: and I shall want nothing. He hath set me in a place of pasture. He hath brought me up, on the water of refreshment: he hath converted my soul. He hath led me on the paths of justice, for his own name's sake. For though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me. Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me. Thou hast prepared a table before me against them that afflict me. Thou hast anointed my head with oil; and my chalice which inebriateth me, how goodly is it! And thy mercy will follow me all the days of my life. And that I may dwell in the house of the Lord unto length of days. — Psalm 23 (22)
The handout sets the psalm beside a painting of the pilgrims on the way to Emmaus. The shepherd who leads us through the dark valley is the same Lord who walked beside the two disciples on the road.
[[art:Angelsatmamre-trinity-rublev-1410.jpg|Andrei Rublev, The Trinity (about 1410): the three visitors to Abraham, an image of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit]]
## Made by love, for love
God did not need to create us. He is perfectly happy and complete in himself. He made us freely, out of pure goodness, so that we could share in his own blessed life (Catechism 1, 293).
That is why every human heart carries a longing that nothing in this world fully satisfies. We were made by the God who is love, and we are made for his love (Catechism 27-30).
> Our hearts are restless until they rest in you. — St. Augustine

And God is not waiting for us to find our own way to him. At every moment of our lives he comes close, calling us to seek him, to know him and to love him (Catechism 1). Like the shepherd of Psalm 23, he is the one who comes looking for us.
## One God, three Persons

There is only one God (Catechism 200-202). Yet God has revealed that his one life is a communion of three Persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 221). We could never have worked this out on our own. We know it because God showed us, by sending his Son, Jesus, and then his Holy Spirit.

This is God's "inmost secret": his very being is love shared between Persons. As the Catechism says, God himself is an eternal exchange of love, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and he has made us to share in that exchange (Catechism 221).

The diagram below, sometimes called the Shield of the Trinity, helps keep this straight. Each Person is fully God. But the Persons are truly distinct: the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Holy Spirit, and the Holy Spirit is not the Father.
[[figure:trinity]]

So we must avoid two mistakes. It is not three gods working together, and it is not one God simply wearing three masks. The Church worships one God in the Trinity, without mixing up the Persons or dividing God's one being. Their glory is equal and their majesty is eternal (Catechism 266).
## What faith is
Faith is our answer to the God who has made himself known. It has two sides (Catechism 150).
- Intellect: with our minds we believe, saying yes to what God has revealed.
- Will: with our hearts we choose to entrust our whole lives to him, the way you would trust a friend with everything.
[[figure:faith]]
Faith is not only agreeing with ideas, and it is not only a feeling. It is both: knowing who God is, and choosing to lean on him.
## Three key elements of prayer
Prayer is how faith becomes a relationship. Three simple elements can shape it:
- Praise: start by focusing on God, not on your problems. This is the "truth zone": God is in control and he loves you. Tell him you love him too.
- Petition: ask for what you and others need. Nothing is too small to bring to him.
- Forgiveness: ask God to forgive your sins, and choose to forgive the people who have hurt you.

> We must speak to God as a friend speaks to his friend, as a servant to his master; now asking some favor, now acknowledging our faults, and communicating to him all that concerns us: our thoughts, our fears, our projects, our desires, and in all things seeking his counsel. — St. Ignatius of Loyola
sessions.reflection: Pray Psalm 23 slowly this week. Where in your life do you need to trust that God is the shepherd walking with you?

deeper.title: Why two creeds?
deeper.text:
A creed is a short summary of what Christians believe. The Church keeps two from the early centuries, and both proclaim faith in the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

The Apostles' Creed is one of the earliest, first used in Rome when people were baptized. We still use it at Baptisms and to begin the Rosary.

The Nicene Creed was first written at the Council of Nicaea in 325 AD to answer questions that had arisen about the Trinity and about whether Jesus is truly God. Its extra detail is about clarity. It is the creed we normally say at Sunday Mass and on major feasts.

sessions.title: Divine Revelation: God seeking us
sessions.summary: God has shown us who he is and his loving plan to save us. It reaches us through Scripture, Tradition and the Church's teaching, all three together.

sources.title: Matthew 16:13-19, the keys of the kingdom
John 16:12-15, the Spirit will guide you into all truth
Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation)
Catechism 50-100: God comes to meet us

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 2
lesson: Session 2 opens with a famous painting by Perugino in the Sistine Chapel: Jesus handing the keys of the kingdom to Peter, the first pope (Matthew 16:18-19). Hold on to that picture. It shows how God makes sure what he revealed is handed on faithfully.

[[art:Entrega de las llaves a San Pedro (Perugino).jpg|Perugino, The Delivery of the Keys (1481-82), Sistine Chapel: Jesus, the key to the kingdom, and Peter, the first pope, as labelled on your sheet]]
## Five things to remember
- Divine Revelation: God revealed himself and his loving plan for humanity, for our salvation.
- Jesus: Christ is the fulfillment of God's revelation.
- Tradition and Scripture: they are the oral and the written handing-on of the faith.
- The Magisterium: the deposit of faith has been entrusted to the Church's teaching office as the authoritative interpreter of Scripture and Tradition.
- All three together: we need Sacred Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium. One cannot stand without the other two.
## God shows himself

"Divine Revelation" means God making himself known. We could never reach God by our own effort alone, so he chose to reveal himself and his loving plan to save us, so that we could know him and love him (Catechism 50-52).

He did this step by step, through deeds and words, across a long story: creation, Abraham, Moses, the kings and prophets of Israel. This story of God gradually saving his people is called salvation history (Catechism 53-64).

That story reaches its high point in Jesus Christ, the Son of God made man. He is not just one more messenger. He is the fullness of Revelation: in him God has said everything he wanted to say (Catechism 65). That is why the Church teaches that no new public revelation is coming before Jesus returns.
## How it reaches us: Scripture and Tradition
Jesus did not hand his apostles a finished book. He taught them, lived with them, and sent them out to preach. What he revealed was passed on in two ways (Catechism 75-79):

- Sacred Tradition: the living handing-on of everything Christ did and taught, first through the apostles' preaching and witness, and then through the Church's doctrine, life and worship (Catechism 76-78).
- Sacred Scripture: the part of that same Revelation the Holy Spirit inspired to be written down, the Bible (Catechism 81).

They are not two competing sources but one stream flowing from the same spring. Nothing in Tradition can contradict Scripture, and Scripture is best understood in the light of the Tradition it came from (Catechism 80-83).
The fullness of the truth is found in Scripture and Tradition together, not in one of them alone.
## Who interprets it: the Magisterium

The apostles entrusted this whole "deposit of faith" to the Church. The Magisterium (from the Latin for "teacher") is the teaching office of the Church: the pope and the bishops in communion with him, the successors of Peter and the apostles. Its job is to interpret God's word faithfully, not to add to it (Catechism 84-86). It serves the word of God; it is not above it.

That is what the keys in the painting mean. Your handout labels it: Jesus, the key to the kingdom, and Peter, the first pope. Jesus gave Peter real authority so that his followers in every century could know they are hearing the true faith and not just someone's opinion.
## The three-legged stool
Scripture, Tradition and the Magisterium work together. Take away any one, and the whole thing topples (Catechism 95).
[[figure:stool]]
Your class note on the drawing: the seat of the stool is the Church. To have the Church you need all three legs. You can't cut one of them.

> Sacred Tradition, Sacred Scripture and the teaching authority of the Church, in accord with God's most wise design, are so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without the others. — Second Vatican Council, Dei Verbum 10
The same passage adds that the one Holy Spirit works through all three, and that each, in its own way, helps bring souls to salvation.
## Complete, yet still unfolding

If everything has been revealed in Jesus, is there anything left to learn? Yes. Jesus promised that the Holy Spirit would guide his Church into all truth (John 16:13). Revelation is complete, but the Church keeps understanding it more deeply over the centuries (Catechism 66).
> When he, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will guide you into all truth. — John 16:13
Public Revelation was complete when the last apostle died. From then on, nothing new needs to be added.

The Catholic writer Mark Mallett (in The Final Confrontation, quoted in your handout) compares it to a flower. Christ gave the apostles the whole "bud" of Revelation, and over the centuries its petals keep opening, bringing greater light and understanding to the Church. He imagines they will keep unfolding for all eternity, as we discover more and more of God's wisdom and splendour. Nothing new is added; what was there all along is seen more clearly.
## Hear it and live it
> Be doers of the word and not hearers only, deluding yourselves. — James 1:22

St. James goes on: if you only listen and do not act, you are like someone who looks at their face in a mirror, walks away, and at once forgets what they look like. But whoever looks closely into the perfect law that sets people free, and keeps doing it instead of forgetting, will be blessed by God in what they do (James 1:22-25).

And this is freedom. Freedom is not doing whatever you want, but doing what you ought to do. If God is a loving Father, he knows what is best for us. Through Divine Revelation, the Catholic Church has been given the tools to help us live in true freedom. The ultimate goal is for us to one day share eternal life with God and our heavenly family. We are not alone: we have the Church on earth and in heaven helping us along the journey of life.

deeper.title: Two words worth knowing
deeper.text:
Salvation history is the story of everything God has done to rescue and draw humanity back to himself: from creation, through Abraham, Moses and the prophets, to Jesus, and on through the Church until he comes again. The Bible is, at heart, this one long story.

Magisterium is the Church's teaching office: the pope and the bishops united with him. When it teaches on faith and morals, it is guarding and explaining what God has already revealed in Scripture and Tradition, never inventing something new.

sessions.reflection: Is there a part of God's word you have heard but not yet put into practice? What is one small step you could take this week?

sessions.title: The Bible: God's love letter
sessions.summary: The Bible is God's love letter to his children: inspired by the Holy Spirit, read with the Church, and meant to be prayed.

sources.title: Read the Bible online (NRSV, the translation of the Canadian Lectionary)
Dei Verbum (Vatican II on Divine Revelation)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 3
lesson: The Bible is God's loving communication with each of us. Scott Hahn, in A Father Who Keeps His Promises (quoted in your handout), calls Scripture one of the most precious family heirlooms we have. It records the highlights of a divine drama: not a dry, impersonal history lesson, and not a set of morality tales where the hero in the white hat beats the villain in the black hat and rides off into the sunset. It is a passionate love story about a God who came to seek and save the lost at great cost to himself. He calls it a long love letter from the Father to his beloved children, still on their earthly pilgrimage.
[[art:Saint Jerome Writing-Caravaggio (1605-6).jpg|Caravaggio, Saint Jerome Writing (about 1606): Jerome translated the Bible into Latin]]
## Inspired by the Holy Spirit
- The Word of God in human words: Scripture is God speaking to us through the language of people (Catechism 101).

- Two authors at once: God is the author of Scripture. He inspired human writers who were real authors too, using their own language, style and abilities, yet they wrote what God wanted written, and nothing more (Catechism 105-106).
- Always true: because the Holy Spirit stands behind what the human authors affirm, Scripture teaches faithfully and without error the truth God wanted written for our salvation (Catechism 107).
## Reading it the Catholic way

Catholics do not read the Bible literalistically, as if every sentence were a newspaper report. We read it literarily: paying attention to what each human author meant to say, and to what God wants to reveal through them (Catechism 109-114).

That means asking about the time and culture it was written in, and the kind of writing it is. The Bible contains history, prophecy, poetry, law, letters and more, and each tells the truth in its own way (Catechism 110). A psalm is read like a song, not like a legal document.
## The four senses of Scripture
An ancient tradition sees two main levels of meaning in Scripture: the literal and the spiritual. The spiritual sense has three parts (Catechism 115-118).
The spiritual sense exists because God's plan is one. Not only the words of Scripture, but the real events and things it describes, can themselves be signs pointing beyond themselves.
- Literal: what the words of Scripture actually mean, found through careful study and explanation of the text (called exegesis). All the other senses are built on this one.
- Allegorical: how events point to Christ. For example, Israel crossing the Red Sea is a sign of Baptism.
- Moral: how the text teaches us to live justly. St. Paul says these things were written "for our instruction" (1 Corinthians 10:11).
- Anagogical: from a Greek word meaning "leading up." How events point to our eternal destiny. Jerusalem, for example, points to the heavenly city.
> The Letter speaks of deeds; Allegory to faith; The Moral how to act; Anagogy our destiny. — Medieval saying, quoted in the Catechism 118
## Which books belong: the canon
All of Scripture tells one story, the story of salvation that reaches its climax in Jesus. The Old Testament prepares for the New, and the New fulfills the Old (Catechism 121-123, 128-129).

Guided by the Holy Spirit through apostolic Tradition, the Church discerned which books belong in the Bible. That complete list is called the canon (Catechism 120): 46 books in the Old Testament and 27 in the New, 73 in all.
The full list of all 73 books, grouped the way your handout groups them, is in "All 73 books" in the Digging deeper section below.
[[figure:canon]]

Most Protestant Bibles have 66 books. After the Protestant Reformation, Martin Luther moved seven Old Testament books into a separate section, and later Protestant Bibles dropped them: Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach (also called Ecclesiasticus), Baruch, and 1 and 2 Maccabees. Parts of two other books went too: chapters 10 to 16 of Esther, and from Daniel the passage 3:24-90 plus chapters 13 and 14. Catholics call these the deuterocanonical books. They were in the Greek Old Testament used by the early Christians, and the Church has always counted them as Scripture.
## How to start reading and praying the Bible
The Church has always seen Scripture as food for Christian life (Catechism 131). St. Jerome put it bluntly: "Ignorance of Scripture is ignorance of Christ" (Catechism 133).
> The Holy Bible is like a mirror before our mind's eye. In it we see our inner face. — Pope St. Gregory the Great
St. Gregory goes on to say that in Scripture we learn both our spiritual flaws and our beauty, and we can see how far we have come and how far we still are from perfection.

- Start with Sunday: you already hear the Word of God at every Mass. Read the Sunday readings ahead of time. Missals such as The Word Among Us and Magnificat give each day's Mass readings with meditations and prayers. Magnificat has its own app; in Canada, make sure you get the Canadian English edition, not the US one, since the readings differ.
- Make it part of daily prayer: read one of the Gospels, a chapter or even a few verses a day. The Psalms are great for prayer too; many are prayers of King David, written in good times and bad.
- Just begin: God speaks to you personally through Scripture. Even one line can bring insight or comfort. The Word of God is for everyone, so do not worry about how much you know.

Mother Angelica, the American nun who founded EWTN, warned against treating the Gospel as just a record of Jesus' life, locked in the past, almost like a divine history book. It is that, she said, but much more: it is a guide for living. Her approach was spiritual: to bring what she read into everyday life, because it is the truth. So you can't just read it like any other book (from Private and Pithy Lessons from the Scriptures).

deeper.title: Covenant: the thread through the whole Bible
deeper.text:
Throughout the Old Testament, God made a series of covenants with the Israelites, his chosen people, from Adam all the way to King David, until the covenant was fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

The word covenant means "to come together" or "to agree." It is a formal, solemn and binding pact between two or more parties, and each side must live up to its end of the bargain. But a biblical covenant is much more than an earthly contract. Scott Hahn names two differences: a covenant rests on a solemn oath, not a private promise, and it gives persons, not just property. Swearing an oath means calling on God's name, placing yourself under his judgment and accepting a curse on yourself if you break your word. Through covenants God forged family bonds with his people in every age. His summary: think covenant, not contract; Father, not judge; family room, not courtroom.

All through the Old Testament, God makes covenants with his people, and each one widens his family: a couple (Adam), a household (Noah), a tribe (Abraham), a nation (Moses), a kingdom (David). Again and again the people break their side of the covenant through disobedience and sin. Because they had sworn oaths, breaking them brought the curse on themselves.

Jesus establishes the New Covenant. He keeps it perfectly, takes on himself the curse of our broken promises, and opens God's family to the whole world. He is the one mediator between God and humanity (1 Timothy 2:5), and the sign of this covenant is the Eucharist: "This cup is the new covenant in my blood" (Luke 22:20).

How to read the chart: the mediator is the person God made each covenant through (Abram was later renamed Abraham). The role is the part he played for the family, the form is how big God's family became, and the sign is the visible mark of that covenant.

[[figure:covenants]]

deeper.title: All 73 books
deeper.text:
## The Old Testament (46 books)

- The Pentateuch (5): Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy.

- Historical books (16): Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, 1 Kings, 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Tobit, Judith, Esther, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees.

- Wisdom books (7): Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, Wisdom, Sirach.

- The Prophets (18): Isaiah, Jeremiah, Lamentations, Baruch, Ezekiel, Daniel, Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi.

## The New Testament (27 books)

- Gospels (4): Matthew, Mark, Luke, John.

- Historical (1): Acts of the Apostles.

- Letters of Paul (13): Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1 Thessalonians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy, Titus, Philemon.

- Other letters (8): Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude.

- Apocalyptic (1): Revelation.

sessions.title: The story of salvation: creation, fall, and redemption
sessions.summary: The whole Bible in three words: Creation, Fall, Redemption. God made us one family, sin broke it, and Jesus gathers us home.

sources.title: Genesis 12:1-3 and 22:15-18: God's promises to Abraham
Pope Benedict XVI, homily at the start of his pontificate (2005)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 4
lesson: Every good story has a beginning, a crisis and a rescue. The Bible is the greatest of them, and it is true: it is the story of God and of us. Its shape fits in three words: Creation, Fall and Redemption. Once you see this shape, every part of Scripture finds its place.

Your Symbolon handout borrows a famous movie title for it: the greatest story ever told. This story, which we profess in the Creed, tells us that life has a purpose and that our own lives have a reason. We are not just spectators watching time go by. From the moment our first parents rebelled, through the Death and Resurrection of Jesus, God has been writing his plan of salvation. Each of us has a God-given role to play in it. If we refuse his loving invitation, the whole world is poorer, because God's story of love is not complete without each one of us.
[[art:Michelangelo - Creation of Adam (cropped).jpg|Michelangelo, The Creation of Adam (about 1512), Sistine Chapel, Vatican]]
[[figure:salvation]]
[[figure:ladder]]
## Creation: made for love

God is perfectly happy in himself. He did not need us. He made us freely, out of sheer goodness, so that we could share his own blessed life (Catechism 1). We were made to know him, to love him and to live with him forever.
> Each of us is the result of a thought of God. Each of us is willed, each of us is loved, each of us is necessary. — Pope Benedict XVI

In the beginning everything was in harmony: the first man and woman were at peace with God, with each other, with themselves and with creation (Catechism 374-376). Think of two lines: a vertical line joining us to God, and a horizontal line joining us to one another. In creation both were whole. Adam and Eve were one united human family, and that unity reflected the unity of God himself (Catechism 376).
## The Fall: love refused

God gave Adam and Eve real freedom, because love that is forced is not love. Tempted by the devil, they stopped trusting God and chose themselves instead of him (Catechism 396-398). They refused the self-giving love they were made for.

Both lines broke at once. The vertical bond with God was cut, and the horizontal bond between people cracked too. Even the harmony between man and woman was broken (Catechism 396): Adam blames Eve, Cain kills Abel, and the family of God scatters into a broken human family (Catechism 400). Sin also brought death into the world. The Church calls this wound original sin.
- Original sin: not a sin we committed, but a wounded human nature we inherited. We are born without the holiness and friendship with God that we were meant to have (Catechism 404-405).
- Concupiscence: the pull toward sin that remains even after Baptism washes original sin away. It is not itself a sin, but it makes the good harder to choose (Catechism 405, 1264).
## Redemption: God comes to rescue
God did not give up on us. Right after the Fall he promised a Saviour (Genesis 3:15). Then, step by step, through covenants, he began gathering his scattered family again.
Your class chart draws it as a rising line. God had a plan to restore humanity to himself and to each other through certain leaders, and each covenant made his family bigger:
- Adam and Eve: a couple.
- Noah: one family.
- Abraham: one tribe.
- Moses: one nation.
- David: one kingdom.
- Jesus: one universal, Catholic Church, the whole family of God.
God made three great promises to Abraham, and the rest of the Old Testament shows him keeping them:
- A great nation: his descendants would become a great nation. Fulfilled when God, through Moses, freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt and made them his people at Sinai.
- A kingdom: fulfilled when King David expanded Israel's borders and it became a kingdom, and God promised that David's throne would last forever.
- A worldwide blessing: God would send the Messiah to gather all the nations back. Fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, who opens God's family to the whole world in the new and everlasting covenant.

In Jesus all three promises meet. The Son of God became man to die for our sins, offering on our behalf the perfect gift of love that restores us to the Father and to each other, making us one family of God (Catechism 457-460). He paid the debt of sin we could not pay and opened the door to eternal life. And he sent the Holy Spirit to fill us with his very life.
## The Church: God's family gathered

Jesus did not come to save us only one by one, as scattered individuals. He founded the universal, Catholic Church to gather the broken human family into the united family of God, a sign and instrument of our union with God and with each other (Catechism 775-776, 830). That is what "catholic" means: universal, sent to everyone (Catechism 830-831).

The Church, the renewed family of God, has three tasks: to proclaim the Gospel, to baptize, and to make disciples of all humanity (Matthew 28:19-20; Catechism 849). After Jesus ascended into heaven, the apostles carried on these three things, and the Church will keep doing them until the end of time, when Jesus comes back to judge the living and the dead. Through his teaching and the sacraments, the Church hands on the graces Jesus won on the Cross, so that we can live like Christ on earth and with him forever in heaven (Catechism 774-776).
## Where we fit in the story

This story is still being written, and we all have a part to play in God's plan of salvation. Every day we are called to choose between good and evil. Jesus calls us toward his love and a life of virtue, and he wants each of us to help spread his love to everyone we meet.

Satan is the chief enemy of everything good. He invites people to live for the world and a life of sin. You either walk toward the light of Christ, or toward the darkness and despair of the evil one. The way out is simple, though not always easy: turn toward the light of Christ, again and again. Each small choice for God is a step back into the family we were made for.

deeper.title: Why the story matters
deeper.text:
Without Creation, we would not know we are loved and made on purpose. Without the Fall, we could not explain why the world, and our own hearts, are so mixed up. Without Redemption, there would be no hope.

People sometimes call the Bible's story the greatest story ever told. It is better than a story, because it is true: God wrote himself into history to bring his children home.

- Catholic: from the Greek kath' holou, "according to the whole": the Church is for every people, place and time (Catechism 830-831).

- Redemption: buying back. Jesus paid the price of our freedom with his own life (Mark 10:45).

sessions.title: Who is Jesus?
sessions.summary: Jesus is truly God and truly man: one divine Person with two natures. The Church guarded this truth against every distortion, because our salvation depends on it.

sources.title: John 14:1-14: the way, the truth and the life
Hebrews 1:1-4: God has spoken through his Son
Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day vigil, Rome (2000)

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 5
lesson: > It is Jesus that you seek when you dream of happiness; he is waiting for you when nothing else you find satisfies you. — Pope St. John Paul II, World Youth Day 2000
[[art:Spas vsederzhitel sinay.jpg|Christ Pantocrator (6th century), St. Catherine's Monastery, Sinai: one face, truly God and truly man]]

The rest of St. John Paul II's words to young people in Rome (August 19, 2000), in short: Jesus is the beauty that attracts you. He is the one who stirs up in you a thirst for fullness that will not let you settle for compromise. He urges you to take off the masks of a false life, and he reads in your heart the most genuine choices you want to make, the ones others try to stifle.

Every person eventually has to answer the question Jesus asked his disciples: "Who do you say that I am?" (Matthew 16:15). Christianity is not first a set of rules or ideas. It is a relationship with a Person.
## God's final Word

For centuries God spoke to his people in many ways through the prophets. In Jesus he spoke his whole Word at once (Hebrews 1:1-2). Christ, the Son of God made man, is the Father's one, perfect and unsurpassable Word; there will be no other word than this one. St. John of the Cross put it beautifully: in giving us his Son, God told us everything, and he has nothing more to say. What he once said in parts through the prophets, he has now said all at once. So anyone who still asks God for some new vision or revelation would be acting foolishly, and even offending him, by not fixing their eyes entirely on Christ (Catechism 65).

- No new public revelation: Christ's covenant is the new and definitive one, and it will never pass away. We do not wait for a new gospel before Jesus comes again in glory. Yet Revelation has not been made completely explicit, so the Church spends the centuries grasping more fully what Jesus has already given (Catechism 66).

- Private revelations: some, like Fatima or Lourdes, are approved by the Church. They do not belong to the deposit of faith, and they cannot improve or complete what Christ revealed; they help people live it more fully in a certain time. Guided by the Magisterium, the sense of the faithful (sensus fidelium) can tell which of them are an authentic call of Christ or his saints. No Catholic is required to believe them (Catechism 67).

- For everyone: God wants all people to be saved and to come to know the truth, which is Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:4). So Christ must be proclaimed to every nation and every person, and God arranged for what he revealed to be handed on whole, to all generations, to the ends of the earth (Catechism 74).
## True God and true man

At the time God chose, the only Son of the Father, the eternal Word and perfect Image of the Father, became flesh without losing his divine nature (Catechism 479). He did not just look human. He became truly one of us while remaining truly God. This is the Incarnation: God taking on flesh (Catechism 464). Because he is true God and true man in one divine Person, he is the one and only mediator between God and humanity (Catechism 480).
[[figure:natures]]

Jesus is one Person, the eternal Son, with two natures, one divine and one human. They are united without being mixed together and without being split apart (Catechism 481). As man he had a real body, a human soul, a human mind that learned, and a human will. His human mind and will were perfectly in tune with, and freely obedient to, the divine mind and will he shares with the Father and the Holy Spirit (Catechism 470-475, 482). He got tired, wept, and felt joy and fear. He is like us in all things but sin (Hebrews 4:15). The Incarnation is the mystery of this wonderful union of the divine and human natures in the one Person of the Word (Catechism 483).
## Why the Church guarded every word

In the first centuries, Christians worked hard to protect and explain the core truth of the Incarnation: that Jesus Christ is one divine Person with two natures. Thinkers who tried to understand it often fell into errors, called heresies. Each one trimmed away part of the mystery and ended up with a Jesus who could not save us. They fall into three groups. The Church's great councils answered them, and that is where the precise words of our Creed come from.
### 1. Heresies that denied or shrank his divine nature

- Arianism (4th century): taught by Arius. The Son of God was not eternal but created, the highest and first of God's creatures, yet not God himself. The first ecumenical council, Nicaea (325), condemned it and confessed that the Son is "begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father" (Catechism 465).
- Adoptionism (3rd century): Jesus was born purely human and was "adopted" by God as his Son, at his baptism or his Resurrection, because of his exceptional holiness and obedience.
### 2. Heresies that denied or shrank his human nature

- Docetism and Gnosticism (1st-2nd centuries): from the Greek dokein, "to seem" or "to appear." Jesus was purely divine and only appeared to have a body, to eat, to suffer and to die on the Cross. The Gnostics saw physical matter as evil, so they rejected the idea that God could take on real flesh (Catechism 465).

- Apollinarianism (4th century): Jesus had a real human body and a living soul, but no human mind; the divine Word took its place. The Church rejected this, because a human being without a human mind is not fully human.

- Monophysitism (5th century): after the Incarnation, Christ's human nature was swallowed up by his divine nature, like a drop of water in the sea. The Council of Chalcedon (451) answered that Christ has two complete natures, divine and human, without confusion or change, in one Person (Catechism 467).
### 3. A heresy that split the union of the two natures

- Nestorianism (5th century): taught by Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople. Jesus was really two persons, a human one and a divine one, joined only by love or purpose. So Nestorius refused to call Mary Theotokos, Mother of God, saying she was only the mother of the human person. The Council of Ephesus (431) condemned this, declaring that the divine Word united a human nature to himself in his one divine Person (the hypostasis), which makes Mary truly the Mother of God (Catechism 466).
## Why it matters

This is not word-games. The truth about who Jesus is is tied to our salvation, which is why the Church still fights false teachings today. If Jesus were not fully God, he would have no power to forgive sins, defeat death and restore humanity's union with God. If he were not fully man, he could not fully enter our human condition, including suffering on our behalf, to heal and restore our human nature. The early Church Fathers summed it up: what was not taken up by Christ was not redeemed.
## Lord, liar, or something worse?

Jesus forgave sins, claimed to be one with the Father, and accepted worship. C.S. Lewis, an Oxford professor, a famous 20th-century defender of the Christian faith and the author of The Chronicles of Narnia, warned against the "really foolish thing" people say: that they accept Jesus as a great moral teacher but not his claim to be God. A mere man who said what Jesus said would not be a great teacher. He would be a lunatic, on the level of a man who says he is a poached egg, or else the Devil of Hell. You must choose: either he was, and is, the Son of God, or a madman or something worse. You can dismiss him as a fool, reject him as a demon, or fall at his feet and call him Lord and God. But the polite middle option of a great human teacher, Lewis says, "He has not left that open to us. He did not intend to."
Jesus answers the question himself: "I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6).
## Meeting him

Archbishop Fulton Sheen, the much-loved TV bishop, made an hour of prayer before the Blessed Sacrament every day of his priesthood. He said that neither knowing theology nor doing good works is enough, on its own, to keep us in love with Christ; both must come from a personal encounter with him. Insight into God comes not only from between the two covers of a book, "but from two bent knees before an altar." He called the Holy Hour an oxygen tank that revives the breath of the Holy Spirit in the middle of the world's stale air. Knowing about Jesus is a start; the goal is to know him, personally, in prayer, Scripture and the sacraments.

deeper.title: Words the Church uses for Jesus
deeper.text:
- Incarnation: from the Latin for "in the flesh." The Son of God became man in the womb of the Virgin Mary (John 1:14).

- Hypostatic union: the theologian's name for two natures united in one divine Person.

- Consubstantial: of the same substance. We say it in the Creed: the Son is God in exactly the same way the Father is.

- Theotokos: Greek for God-bearer. Calling Mary the Mother of God is really a statement about who Jesus is.

- Christ: Greek for Messiah, "the anointed one." It is a title, not a surname.

sessions.reflection: Jesus asks you, not just the apostles: "Who do you say that I am?" How would you answer today? Try spending fifteen quiet minutes with him this week, in a church if you can.

sessions.title: The Paschal Mystery
sessions.summary: The Paschal Mystery is Jesus' passion, death, resurrection and ascension: how he restored our friendship with God, and how he invites us to share in it.

sources.title: 1 Peter 3:18-19 and 4:6: preaching to the dead

sessions.ref: Symbolon Part 1: Knowing the Faith · Session 6
lesson: The Paschal Mystery is the mystery of Jesus' death and resurrection. It is the centre of the whole faith: everything before it points toward it, and everything after it flows from it.
[[art:Cristo crucificado.jpg|Diego Velázquez, Christ Crucified (about 1632), Prado Museum, Madrid]]
## The cross was shocking

Perhaps the cross has become almost too familiar. We see crosses everywhere, on walls, steeples and necklaces, so it is easy to forget that in the ancient world it was a horrifying image. Crucifixion was the cruelest and most shameful execution Rome had. A Roman wearing a cross around his neck as jewellery would have seemed as bizarre and shocking to his neighbours as someone today wearing a little electric chair. Yet the cross is the main symbol of our faith, because through Jesus' death on that instrument of torture he gave us the gift of salvation and eternal life (Symbolon).
## Why "Paschal"?

Pascha is the Greek form of the Hebrew word for Passover. At the first Passover the blood of a lamb saved Israel's firstborn, and God led his people out of slavery in Egypt. Jesus is the new Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). By his passion, death, resurrection and ascension, he leads us out of slavery to sin and death (Catechism 571).

We proclaim this at every Mass: "We proclaim your Death, O Lord, and profess your Resurrection until you come again." Beneath it all is one simple reality: Jesus gave himself completely, in love, to the Father on our behalf, to restore our relationship with God. And by his death on the cross, Jesus also shows us that we are called to the same sacrificial love, the love that leads to true happiness here on earth and eternal joy in the next life.
## Why did Jesus die for our sins?
[[figure:bridge]]
- A real gap between God and humanity: because of sin there was a true break between God the Father and man. Sin is not a small mistake. It broke our friendship with God, the very source of life.
- We cannot overcome this gap on our own: it is not humanly possible to bridge it. God is infinite, and only a divine, supernatural act, one of infinite worth, could repair it.

- God becomes man to overcome sin: Jesus became the living sacrifice that the Old Testament sacrifices only foreshadowed. He took all our sins on himself, freely, to free us from sin. Because he was both human and divine, he was able to do it: as man he could stand in our place, and as God his offering had infinite worth (Catechism 613-616).
No one took Jesus' life from him; he laid it down freely (John 10:18). The cross is not a picture of an angry God, but of a love that would go all the way for us.
## He descended to the dead
In the Creed we say Jesus "descended into hell." This does not mean the hell of the damned. It means the realm of the dead, which the Hebrews called Sheol and the Greeks Hades (Catechism 633).

Before Christ, all who died, whether evil or good, were deprived of the vision of God, waiting for the Messiah. Jesus, his human soul still united to his divine Person, went down to them. He did not go to free the damned or destroy the hell of damnation, but to open heaven's gates to the just who had gone before him (Catechism 632-637). This descent brings the Gospel of salvation to its complete fulfillment. It is the last phase of Jesus' mission as Messiah: short in time, but vast in meaning. On Holy Saturday his saving work reached all people of all times and places. Everyone, from the beginning of creation to the end of time, is brought into this redemption (Catechism 633-634).
## He rose from the dead

On the third day Jesus rose, truly and bodily. The tomb was empty, and he ate and spoke with his disciples, who were willing to die rather than deny it. St. Paul says that if Christ has not been raised, our faith is in vain (1 Corinthians 15:14).

By his death Jesus frees us from sin; by his resurrection he opens for us the way to a new life in him, so that we may become sons and daughters of God and have eternal life (Catechism 654). Jesus has raised us up to a new life! He has also opened the doors to heaven: eternal life with God and with all who have gone before us.
## Sharing in his cross

Jesus invites us into his death and resurrection. We can unite our whole lives with his cross: our daily work, our joys and our sufferings (Catechism 618). The cross and resurrection are the centre of history, and they are meant to be the centre of each of our lives too.
We will all suffer in some way during our lives; no one can avoid it. So the question should not be "Will I suffer?" but rather "What will I do when I suffer?"
- True love is always sacrificial: it is selfless, and always focused on God and others.
- Living only for yourself shrinks you: you become selfish, in denial of your own mortality and your true purpose.
- Suffering can be offered: our pain becomes a chance to unite ourselves with the suffering of Jesus, and to offer it for others (Colossians 1:24). Catholics sometimes call this "offering it up."
## A prayer to Christ Crucified
Your handout ends with this prayer by St. Thérèse of Lisieux. You can find it in Pray, and in the prayers listed with this session, so you can read it, listen to it and learn it.

St. Thérèse loved this image of empty hands. We come to the cross with nothing of our own to boast of, and there the empty are filled: Christ's hands, emptied for us, pour out mercy, and our hands, emptied for him and for others, are filled with his love.

deeper.title: The Triduum: three days at the heart of the year
deeper.text:
The Paschal Mystery is celebrated every Sunday, and above all in the Easter Triduum, the three holiest days of the Church year.

- Holy Thursday: the Mass of the Lord's Supper, when Jesus gives us the Eucharist and the priesthood, and washes his disciples' feet.

- Good Friday: the Celebration of the Lord's Passion. There is no Mass; we venerate the cross.

- Holy Saturday and the Easter Vigil: the Church waits at the tomb, then lights the new fire and sings the Exsultet. At the Vigil, those finishing RCIA are baptized, confirmed and receive their First Communion.

The Paschal Mystery is where your own journey is heading.
